{{RunningHeader|tester|6252|testimony}}{{smaller block|Causing his servant to leave him unusually one morning, locking himselfe in, he strangled himselfe with his cravatt upon the bed-''tester''.{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 18, 1673.}}}} ¶ '''testiere''' (tes-ti-ãr′), ''n.'' [OF.: see ''tester''2.] A piece of armor for a horse, covering the head and differing (b) In ''arch.'', a flat canopy, as over a pulpit or a tomb. [[File:century v08 p0056 c1f1.png|center|111px]] {{c|Testiere. (From Viollet-le-Duc's "Dict. du Mobilier français.")}} {{smaller block|A ''testor'' of scarlet embroidered with a counterpoint of silksay belonging to the same. {{right|''Strype'', Eccles. Mem. (ed. 1822), II. i. 201.}}}} 2†. A head-piece; a helmet. {{smaller block|The sheeldes brighte, ''testers'' and trappures. {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight's Tale, l. 1642.}}}} '''Half-tester bedstead''', {{smaller|a bedstead having a canopy of about half its length, and therefore supported by the posts at the head only. See ''bedstead''.}} '''tester'''3 (tes′tėr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''testern'', ''testerne'', ''testorn'', also ''testril'', altered forms (later reduced to ''tester'', in conformity with ''tester''2) of ''teston'': see ''teston''. Hence ult. ''tizzy''.] A name given to the shillings coined by Henry VIII., and to sixpences later (compare ''teston''); also, in modern slang, a sixpence. {{smaller block|There 's a ''tester''; Nay, now I am a wooer, I must be bounteful. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man's Fortune, iii. 3.}}}} and differing from the chamfron in covering the head more completely, having ear-pieces, etc. '''testif†''', ''a.'' Middle English form of ''testy''. '''testificate''' (tes-tif′i-kạ̄t), ''n.'' [< L. ''testificatus'', pp. of ''testificari'', testify: see ''testify''.] In ''Scots law'', a solemn written assertion, not on procedure. {{smaller block|They say he that has lost his wife and sixpence has lost a ''tester''. {{right|''Swift'', Polite Conversation, i.}}}} {{smaller block|The demand on thy humanity will surely rise to a ''tester''. {{right|''Lamb'', Chimney-Sweepers.}}}} '''tester-cloth''' (tes′tėr-klôth), ''n.'' The material used to cover the frame of the tester and form the canopy of a four-post bedstead. '''testere†''', ''n.'' [See ''tester''2.] Same as ''testiere''. '''testern†''' (tes′tėrn), ''n.'' Same as ''tester''3. '''testern†''' (tes′tėrn), ''v. t.'' [< ''testern'', ''n.''] To present with a testern or sixpence. {{smaller block|To testify your bounty, I thank you, you have ''testerned'' me; in requital whereof, henceforth carry your letter yourself. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 1. 153.}}}} '''testes''', ''n.'' Plural of ''testis''. '''test-glass''' (test′glȧs), ''n.'' A small glass vessel, {{smaller block|He had deposited this ''testificate'' and confession, with the day and date of the said marriage, with his lawful superior Boniface, Abbot of Saint Mary's. ''Scott'', Abbot, xxviii.}} '''testification''' (tes″ti-fi-kā′shọn), ''n.'' [< OF. ''testification'' = Sp. ''testificacion'' = Pg. ''testificação'' = It. ''testificazione'', < L. ''testificatio''(''n''-), testifying, < ''testificari'', testify: see ''testify''.] The act of testifying, or giving testimony or evidence; a witnessing; testimony; evidence. {{smaller block|Those heavenly mysteries wherein Christ imparteth himself unto us, and giveth visible ''testification'' of our blessed communion with him. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 36.}}}} '''testificator''' (tes′ti-fi-kā-tọr), ''n.'' [< L. as if *''testificator'', < ''testificari'', testify: see ''testify''.] One who testifies; one who gives witness or evidence; a witness. [[File:century v08 p0056 c1f2.png|center|180px]] {{c|Test-glasses.}} '''testifier''' (tes′ti-fī-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''testify'' + ''-er''1.] One who testifies; one who gives testimony or bears witness to anything; a witness. ''Evelyn'', True Religion, II. 196. '''testify''' (tes′ti-fī), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''testified'', ppr. ''testifying''. [< ME. ''testifien'', < OF. ''testifier'' = Sp. Pg. ''testificar'' = It. ''testificare'', < L. ''testificari'', bear witness, < ''testis'', a witness, + ''facere'', make (see ''-fy'').] I. ''intrans.'' 1. To bear witness; make declaration, especially for the purpose of communicating to others a knowledge of some matter not known to them, or for the purpose of establishing some fact. {{smaller block|Jesus . . . needed not that any should ''testify'' of man, for he knew what was in man. {{right|John ii. 25.}}}} {{smaller block|The eye was placed where one ray should fall, that it might ''testify'' of that particular ray. {{right|''Emerson'', Self-Reliance.}}}} 2. In ''law'', to give testimony, under oath or solemn affirmation, in a cause depending before a court. {{smaller block|One witness shall not ''testify'' against any person to cause him to die. {{right|Num. xxxv. 30.}}}} {{smaller block|However many nations and generations of men are brought into the witness-box, they cannot ''testify'' to anything which they do not know. {{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, II. 200.}}}} 3. To serve as evidence; be testimony or proof. {{smaller block|Ah, but some natural notes about her body, Above ten thousand meaner moveables, Would ''testify'', to enrich mine inventory. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 2. 30.}}}} elements of the semen; a testis.—{{smaller|'''Cooper's irritable testicle,''' a testicle affected with neuralgia.}} '''testicond''' (tes′ti-kond), ''a.'' [< L. ''testis,'' testicle, + ''condere,'' hide, conceal.] Having the testes concealed—that is, not contained in an external pouch or scrotum. {{smaller|Most animals are testicond, but the word denotes more particularly mammals of this character, as the cetaceans and some others.}} '''testicular''' (tes-tik′ū-lär), ''a.'' [= F. ''testiculaire'' = It. ''testicolare,'' < L. ''testiculus,'' testicle: see ''testicle.''] 1. Of or pertaining to a testicle or testis: as, ''testicular'' inflammation.—2. In ''bot.,'' same as ''testiculate.''—{{smaller|'''Testicular artery,''' the spermatic artery.—'''Testicular cord.''' Same as ''spermatic cord'' (which see, under ''cord''1).—'''Testicular cyst,''' a retention-cyst of a seminal tubule. Also called ''seminal cyst.''—'''Testicular duct,''' the vas deferens.—'''Testicular veins,''' small veins collecting the blood from the testes, and emptying into the spermatic veins.}} '''testiculate''' (tes-tik′ū-lāt), ''a.'' [< LL. ''testiculatus,'' having testicles, shaped like a testicle, < L. ''testiculus,'' testicle: see ''testis.''] 1. Of the rounded or ovoid shape of a testicle.—2. Having a pair of testicle-like formations.—3. In ''bot.'': (''a'') Shaped like a testicle. (''b'') Having a pair of organs so shaped, as the tubers of ''Orchis mascula.'' Also ''testicular, testiculated.'' '''testiculated''' (tes-tik′ū-lā-ted), ''a.'' [< ''testiculate'' + ''-ed''2.] In ''bot.,'' same as ''testiculate.'' '''II.''' ''trans.'' 1. To bear witness to; affirm or declare as fact or truth. {{smaller block|We speak that we do know, and ''testify'' that we have seen, and ye receive not our witness. {{right|John iii. 11.}} I ''testified'' the pleasure I should have in his company. {{right|''Goldsmith,'' Vicar, iii.}}}} 2. In ''law,'' to state or declare under oath or affirmation, as a witness, before a tribunal.—3. To give evidence of; evince; demonstrate; show. {{smaller block|Prayers are those "calves of men's lips," those most gracious and sweet odours, . . . which being carried up into heaven do best ''testify'' our dutiful affection. {{right|''Hooker,'' Eccles. Polity, v. 23.}}}} 4. To make known; publish or declare freely. {{smaller block|''Testifying'' both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ. {{right|Acts xx. 21.}}}} '''testill''' (tes′til), ''n.'' [< NL. *''testilla,'' dim. of L. ''testa,'' a potsherd: see ''test''2.] In ''bot.,'' same as ''frustule.'' '''testily''' (tes′ti-li), ''adv.'' In a testy manner; fretfully; peevishly; with petulance. '''testimonial''' (tes-ti-mō′ni-ạl), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< F. ''testimonial'' = Sp. ''testimonial'' = It. ''testimoniale,'' < LL. ''testimonialis,'' of or pertaining to testimony, < L. ''testimonium,'' testimony: see ''testimony.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Relating to or containing testimony. {{smaller block|A clerk does not exhibit to the bishop letters missive or ''testimonial'' testifying his good behaviour. {{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon.}}}} {{smaller block|'''Testimonial proof''', proof by testimony of a witness, as distinguished from evidence afforded by a document.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' '''1†.''' A will; a testament. {{smaller block|To dispossesse
His children of his goodes, & give her all
By his last dying ''testimoniall.'' {{right|''Times' Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 135.}}}} '''2†.''' A certificate; a warrant. {{smaller block|That none of the said reteyned persons in Husbandrye, or in any the Artes or Sciences above remembred, after the tyme of his Reteynor expired, shall departe foorthe of one Cytye, Towne, or Parishe to another, . . . onles he have a ''Testimoniall'' under the Seale of the said Citie or Towne Corporate. {{right|''Laws of Elizabeth'' (1562), quoted in Ribton-Turner's [Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 101.}}}} '''3†.''' A mark; token; evidence; proof. {{smaller block|A signe and solemne ''testimoniall'' of the religious observance which they carried respectively to the whole element of fire. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 613.}}}} '''4†.''' A statement; a declaration; testimony. {{smaller block|I must giue the Kings Kingdomes a caueat here, concerning vagabonding Greekes, and their counterfeit ''Testimonials:'' True it is, there is no such matter as these lying Rascals report vnto you. {{right|''W. Lithgow'', Travels, iii.}}}} '''5.''' A writing certifying to one's character, conduct, or qualifications; a certificate of worth, attainment, excellence, value, genuineness, etc.—'''6.''' A tangible expression of respect, esteem, admiration, appreciation or acknowledgment of services, or the like. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|The late lamented O'Connell, . . . over whom a grateful country has raised such a magnificent ''testimonial.'' {{right|''Thackeray'', Virginians, xi.}}}} {{smaller block|The portrait was intended as a ''testimonial'', "expressive . . . of the eminent services of Mr. Boxsious in promoting and securing the prosperity of the town." {{right|''W. Collins'', After Dark, p. 45.}}}} '''Testimonial of the great seal.''' Same as ''quarter-seal.'' '''testimonialize''' (tes-ti-mō′ni-al-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''testimonialized'', ppr. ''testimonializing.'' [< ''testimonial'' + ''-ize.''] To present with a testimonial. [Rare.] {{smaller block|People were ''testimonialising'' his wife. {{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, lxiii.}}}} '''testimony''' (tes′ti-mō-ni), ''n.''; pl. ''testimonies'' (-niz). [= F. ''temoin'' = Pr. ''testimoni'' = Sp. ''testimonio'' = Pg. ''testimunho'' = It. ''testimone'', ''testimonio'', < L. ''testimonium'', testimony, < ''testis'', a witness: see ''test''3.] '''1.''' Witness; evidence; proof or demonstration of some fact. {{smaller block|I'll give you all noble remembrances,
As ''testimonies'' 'gainst reproach and malice,
That you departed lov'd. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Nice Valour, iv. 1.}} I swear by truth and knighthood that I gave
No cause, not willingly, for such a love:
To this I call my friends in ''testimony.'' {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}} '''2.''' In ''law'', the statement or declaration of a witness; oral evidence; a solemn statement or declaration under oath or affirmation, made as evidence before a tribunal or an officer for the purposes of evidence; a statement or statements made in proof of something.—'''3.''' Tenor of declarations or statements made or witness borne; declaration: as, the ''testimony'' of history. {{smaller block|As to the fruits of Sodom, fair without, and full of ashes within, I saw nothing of them; tho', from the ''testimonies'' we have, something of this kind has been produced. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|Who trusts To human ''testimony'' for a fact Gets this sole fact—himself is proved a fool. {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 324.}}}} 4. The act of bearing witness; open attestation; profession. {{smaller block|Thou . . . for the ''testimony'' of truth hast borne Universal reproach. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 33.}}}} {{smaller block|The two first [Quakers in New England] that sealed their ''testimony'' with their blood were William Robinson, merchant of London, and Marmaduke Stevenson, a countryman of Yorkshire. {{right|''Sewel'', History of the Quakers (1856), I. 290.}}}} 5. A declaration or protest. {{smaller block|Shake off the dust under your feet, for a ''testimony'' against them. {{right|Mark vi. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|Alice Rose was not one to tolerate the coarse, careless talk of such a woman as Mrs. Brunton without uplifting her voice in many a ''testimony'' against it. {{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia's Lovers, xxxix.}}}} 6. In ''Scrip.'': (''a'') The law of God in general; the Scriptures. {{smaller block|The ''testimony'' of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. {{right|Ps. xix. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''testimonies'' of God are true, the ''testimonies'' of God are perfect, the ''testimonies'' of God are all sufficient unto that end for which they were given. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, ii. 8.}}}} (''b'') Specifically, the two tables of the law (tables of the testimony); the decalogue.
